name: Indigo Blue
lede: Indigo Blue is a mid greyish blue with three lives: the name of the dye's own colorant, a numbered entry in Werner's mineral color chart, and the everyday blue of denim.

sections.title: Three things called indigo blue
sections.body:
Books use *indigo blue* for the colorant itself. Balfour-Paul writes that every indigo-bearing plant, from tropical *Indigofera* to European woad, yields the same indigo blue chemically [5]. The precursor is indican, a compound present in the leaves, and processing turns it into the blue colorant [6]. Schunk, writing in the 1850s, already called the substance indigo-blue and thought it so peculiar that it almost formed a class of its own among organic bodies [7]. Paterson's dictionary gives the phrase as a dark, sometimes purplish blue and also as the name of the dye [14].

The second use is the chart color. Our swatch, #4F638D, comes from Werner's nomenclature (no. 26 among the blues), Ridgway's color plates of 1886 and 1912, and the German RAL system, which lists a nearly identical RAL 5023, called Distant Blue [18]. The swatch is a mid blue with a slight grey, not a dark one [18].

The third is the blue of workwear. The dye's actual color on a fiber is far darker than this swatch, which is why the neighboring [[indigo-dye]] and the main [[indigo]] article exist [18]. The chart color is nearest to [[denim]], a faded rather than a freshly dyed blue [18][19].

sections.title: Werner's number 26
sections.body:
Indigo Blue entered color vocabulary through mineralogy [1]. Abraham Werner's scheme of named colors, in the Scottish edition of Patrick Syme (1814, revised 1821), puts Indigo Blue at number 26 in the blues [1][18]. Syme's note on the entry makes clear that the name belonged to Werner's own original list rather than to Syme's additions [3].

Baty reports that the 1821 edition kept the name Indigo Blue but gave it an amended recipe, and that the old 1814 recipe went to a new entry, Scotch Blue [2]. Baty prints the recipe for Indigo Blue as Berlin blue with a little black and a small share of apple green [3]. In other words, a mineralogist's idea of the color was a mixture of [[prussian-blue]], black and green, not indigo itself [3].

Werner's real-world example for the color was a mineral, blue copper ore (azurite) [18]. Baty's illustrated version pairs it with the blue cuckooshrike and the Bavarian gentian, but those are Baty's own choices of picture, not Werner's list [3]. The term was already in use elsewhere: by 1813 an English treatise on gems called some tourmalines indigo blue [1].

Indigo Blue also served as a building block in this system [4]. Syme describes ink black as velvet black with a little indigo blue, crimson red as carmine with a little indigo blue, and pansy purple as indigo blue with carmine red and a touch of black [4].

sections.title: The dye and the factory
sections.body:
The chemistry was settled late. Adolf von Baeyer worked out the structure of indigo in 1865, and it took until 1897 before the German firm BASF launched a synthetic product, sold as Indigo Pure [8]. The firm is said to have spent eighteen million gold marks on the research, more than its capital at the time [8].

Natural and synthetic indigo are the same blue molecule [9]. Balfour-Paul reports the claim that natural dye has more body, and that a reddish tinge can come from the companion compound indirubin, which is why the two are often said to differ [9]. The difference is in the impurities, not the blue [9].

Before then the dye had a bad reputation in Europe [17]. Woad was a protected local industry, imported indigo was fought with laws, and the new dye was confused with logwood, whose false indigo blue was unstable [17]. Nelson passes on that the dye was once called the devil's dye in that fight, though she does not give a source for the phrase [15].

sections.title: A blue that fades into itself
sections.body:
One reason indigo blue became the standard blue of cloth is that it ages well. Balfour-Paul says it keeps its hue even as it grows paler, whereas yellows are fugitive and most other colors turn duller [10]. Old tapestries show this directly. Their green foliage was woven from blue and yellow wools, and when the yellow vanished the leaves reverted to blue, an effect known as preferential fading [10]. The only original color of the Bayeux tapestry that remains true, according to Balfour-Paul, is the indigo blue of its woad-dyed wools [10].

The same durability is why indigo cloth survives in excavations. Balfour-Paul lists indigo-blue Chinese designs on silk fragments from near Dunhuang dated between 206 BC and AD 220, resist-dyed wool from a Roman desert fort, and Indian cotton fragments radiocarbon-dated to about the year 895 [12]. The Ardabil carpet in London has indigo-blue fields that show the dye lasting centuries [11].

sections.title: Indigo blue as a cloth color
sections.body:
In many places indigo blue is the ground against which other colors are placed. Japanese paste-resist work used indigo blue as the classic ground color [13]. In Sindh and Kutch, the block-printed ajrakh cloth is built from alizarin red and indigo blue, and the name is a corruption of the Arabic and Persian word for blue, *azraq* [13]. In the Mahdist army of Sudan, the patches on a tunic, often indigo blue, stood for humility [13].

For most people today the name means jeans. By Pastoureau's account, Levi Strauss began between 1860 and 1865 to replace canvas with denim, a twilled fabric dyed with indigo [15]. St Clair reports that the global denim industry, dominated by classic indigo blue, was worth $54 billion in 2011 [16]. Balfour-Paul, writing before that, says indigo-blue jeans had united cultures worldwide [5].

This is also the clue for the swatch. A pair of jeans is darkest when new and pales through washing; the chart color here, the one nearest to [[denim]], is the middle stage [18][19].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, as photographed, the swatch color covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 97 works, or 0.41 per cent [19]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is a look-alike hue, not a dye test [19].

It is a twentieth-century color in painting. Our archive finds it in 30 of 1,674 works from the 1900s, or 1.8 per cent, about four times the archive's rate, and in 6 of 237 works from the 1920s [19]. [[painter:henri-matisse|Matisse]] holds it in 5 of his 50 works, among them [[painting:commons-Q1853880|Blue Nude IV]], and [[painter:vilhelm-lundstr-m|Lundstrøm]] in 3 of 17 [19]. Other large examples are [[painting:cma-172828|Holiday on the Hudson]] by George Luks and [[painting:commons-Q64211180|Harlequin]] by Cézanne [19].

The earliest match is a 1350 Madonna and Child Enthroned, 471 years before the name appears in our sources, so it is a look-alike hue, not proof of indigo [19][18]. In a painting the color most often sits in the middle tones (63 per cent) or shadows (33 per cent), almost never in the highlights (4 per cent) [19].

In printed English, the phrase *indigo blue* peaks around 1879 and had fallen to about a quarter of that peak by 1960 [20]. Where to look: in a faded pair of jeans, or in an old green tapestry whose foliage has gone blue, where the yellow has left and only the indigo remains [10].

questions.q: True or false: natural and synthetic indigo are different molecules.

openers: Syme's recipe for Werner's Indigo Blue contains no indigo: it is Berlin blue, a little black and a touch of apple green [3].
Old tapestries with blue leaves lost their yellow, and indigo outlasted it [10].

issues: Baty p.94 recipe attributed to current Syme text; 1814 vs 1821 recipe swap per Baty p.28
Werner dating given as 'late eighteenth century' from context, not a cited date
Archive match is look-alike, not dye test
